arXiv:1410.4079v1 [math.AP] 15 Oct 2014

Blow-up results for a strongly perturbed semilinear heat equation: Theoretical analysis and numerical method

V. T. Nguyen and H. Zaag
Université Paris 13, Sorbonne Paris Cité,
LAGA, CNRS (UMR 7539), F-93430, Villetaneuse, France. Note: This author is supported by the ERC Advanced Grant no. 291214, BLOWDISOL and by the ANR project ANAÉ ref. ANR-13-BS01-0010-03.
Abstract

We consider a blow-up solution for a strongly perturbed semilinear heat equation with Sobolev subcritical power nonlinearity. Working in the framework of similarity variables, we find a Lyapunov functional for the problem. Using this Lyapunov functional, we derive the blow-up rate and the blow-up limit of the solution. We also classify all asymptotic behaviors of the solution at the singularity and give precisely blow-up profiles corresponding to these behaviors. Finally, we attain the blow-up profile numerically, thanks to a new mesh-refinement algorithm inspired by the rescaling method of Berger and Kohn [5]. Note that our method is applicable to more general equations, in particular those with no scaling invariance.

Keywords: Blow-up, Lyapunov functional, asymptotic behavior, blow-up profile, semilinear heat equation, lower order term.

1 Introduction

We are concerned in this paper with blow-up phenomena arising in the following nonlinear heat problem:

{ut=Δ​u+|u|p−1​u+h⁡(u),u(.,0)=u0∈L∞​(ℝn),\left\{\begin{array}[]{rcl}u_{t}&=&\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u+h(u),\\ u(.,0)&=&u_{0}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\end{array}\right. (1)

where u⁡(t):x∈ℝn→u⁡(x,t)∈ℝu(t):x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\to u(x,t)\in\mathbb{R} and Δ\Delta stands for the Laplacian in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. The exponent p>1p>1 is subcritical (that means that p<n+2n−2p<\frac{n+2}{n-2} if n≥3n\geq 3) and hh is given by

h⁡(z)=μ​|z|p−1​zloga⁡(2+z2),with​a>0,μ∈ℝ.h(z)=\mu\dfrac{|z|^{p-1}z}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})},\quad\text{with}\;\;a>0,\;\mu\in\mathbb{R}. (2)

By standard results, the problem (1) has a unique classical solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) in L∞​(ℝn)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n}), which exists at least for small times. The solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) may develop singularities in some finite time. We say that u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) blows up in a finite time TT if u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) satisfies (1) in ℝb×[0,T)\mathbb{R}^{b}\times[0,T) and

limt→T‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(ℝn)=+∞.\lim_{t\to T}\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}=+\infty.

TT is called the blow-up time of u⁡(x,t)u(x,t). In such a blow-up case, a point b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is called a blow-up point of u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) if and only if there exist (xn,tn)→(b,T)(x_{n},t_{n})\to(b,T) such that |u⁡(xn,tn)|→+∞|u(x_{n},t_{n})|\to+\infty as n→+∞n\to+\infty.

In the case μ=0\mu=0, the equation (1) is the semilinear heat equation,

ut=Δ​u+|u|p−1​u.u_{t}=\Delta u+|u|^{p-1}u. (3)

Problem (3) has been addressed in different ways in the literature. The existence of blow-up solutions has been proved by several authors (see Fujita [12], Levine [27], Ball [3]). Consider u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) a solution of (3) which blows up at a time TT. The very first question to be answered is the blow-up rate, i.e. there are positive constants C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} such that

C1​(T−t)−1p−1≤‖u⁡(t)‖L∞​(ℝn)≤C2​(T−t)−1p−1,∀t∈(0,T).C_{1}(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\leq\|u(t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\leq C_{2}(T-t)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}},\quad\forall t\in(0,T). (4)

The lower bound in (4) follows by a simple argument based on Duhamel’s formula (see Weissler [36]). For the upper bound, Giga and Kohn proved (4) in [13] for 1<p<3​n+83​n−41<p<\frac{3n+8}{3n-4} or for non-negative initial data with subcritical pp. Then, this result was extended to all subcritiacal pp without assuming non-negativity for initial data u0u_{0} by Giga, Matsui and Sasayama in [15]. The estimate (4) is a fundamental step to obtain more information about the asymptotic blow-up behavior, locally near a given blow-up point b^\hat{b}. Giga and Kohn showed in [14] that for a given blow-up point b^∈ℝn\hat{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

limt→T(T−t)1p−1​u​(b^+y​T−t,t)=±κ,\lim_{t\to T}(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(\hat{b}+y\sqrt{T-t},t)=\pm\kappa,

where κ=(p−1)−1p−1\kappa=(p-1)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}, uniformly on compact sets of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.
This result was specified by Filippas ans Liu [11] (see also Filippas and Kohn [10]) and Velázquez [34], [35] (see also Herrero and Velázquez [22], [24], [21]). Using the renormalization theory, Bricmont and Kupiainen showed in [6] the existence of a solution of (3) such that

‖(T−t)1p−1​u​(b^+z​(T−t)​|log⁡(T−t)|,t)−f0​(z)‖L∞​(ℝn)→0ast→T,\left\|(T-t)^{\frac{1}{p-1}}u(\hat{b}+z\sqrt{(T-t)|\log(T-t)|},t)-f_{0}(z)\right\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{n})}\to 0\quad\text{as}\quad t\to T, (5)

where

f0​(z)=κ​(1+p−14​p​|z|2)−1p−1.f_{0}(z)=\kappa\left(1+\frac{p-1}{4p}|z|^{2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}. (6)

Merle and Zaag in [29] obtained the same result through a reduction to a finite dimensional problem. Moreover, they showed that the profile (6) is stable under perturbations of initial data (see also [8], [9] and [28]).

In the case where the function hh satisfies

j=0,1,|h(j)​(z)|≤M⁡(|z|p−jloga⁡(2+z2)+1),|h′′​(z)|≤M​|z|p−2loga⁡(2+z2),j=0,1,\;\;|h^{(j)}(z)|\leq M\left(\frac{|z|^{p-j}}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})}+1\right),\quad|h^{\prime\prime}(z)|\leq M\frac{|z|^{p-2}}{\log^{a}(2+z^{2})}, (7)

with a>1a>1 and M>0M>0, we proved in [32] the existence of a Lyapunov functional in similarity variables for the problem (1) which is a crucial step in deriving the estimate (4). We also gave a classification of possible blow-up behaviors of the solution when it approaches to singularity. In [33], we constructed a blow-up solution of the problem (1) satisfying the behavior described in (5) in the case where hh satisfies the first estimate in (7) or hh is given by (2).

In this paper, we aim at extending the results of [32] to the case a∈(0,1]a\in(0,1]. As we mentioned above, the first step is to derive the blow-up rate of the blow-up solution. As in [15] and [32], the key step is to find a Lyapunov functional in similarity variables for equation (1). More precisely, we introduce for all b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n} (bb may be a blow-up point of uu or not) the following similarity variables:

Remark 2.

In our previous paper [32], we were unable to get this result in the case where hh satisfies (7) with a∈(0,1]a\in(0,1]. Here, by taking the particular form of the perturbation (see (2)), we are able to overcome technical difficulties in order to derive the result.

Remark 3.

From 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁i​i)ii) of Theorem 2, we would naturally try to find an equivalent for w−κw-\kappa as s→+∞s\to+\infty. A posteriori from our results in Theorem 3, we see that in all cases ‖w−κ‖Lρ2∼Csa′\|w-\kappa\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}\sim\frac{C}{s^{a^{\prime}}} with a′=max⁡{a,1}a^{\prime}=\max\{a,1\}. This is indeed a new phenomenon observed in our equation (1), and which is different from the case of the unperturbed semilinear heat equation where either w−κ≡0w-\kappa\equiv 0, or ‖w−κ‖Lρ2∼Cs\|w-\kappa\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}\sim\frac{C}{s} or ‖w−κ‖Lρ2∼C​e(1−m/2)​s\|w-\kappa\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}\sim Ce^{(1-m/2)s} for some even m≥4m\geq 4. This shows the originality of our paper. In our case, linearizing around κ\kappa would keep us trapped in the 1s\frac{1}{s} scale. In order to escape that scale, we forget the explicit function κ\kappa which is not a solution of equation (9), and linearizing instead around the non-explicit function ϕ\phi, which happens to be an exact solution of (9). This way, we escape the 1s\frac{1}{s} scale and reach exponentially decreasing order.

Remark 4.

As in the unperturbed case (h≡0h\equiv 0), we expect that (22) is stable (see the previous remarks, particularly the paragraph after (5)), and (24) should correspond to unstable behaviors (the unstable of (24) was proved only in one space dimension by Herrero and Velázquez in [23] and [25]). While remarking numerical simulation for equation (1) in one space dimension (see Section 4.2 below), we see that the numerical solutions exhibit only the behavior (22), we could never obtain the behavior (24). This is probably due to the fact that the behavior (24) is unstable.

At the end of this work, we give numerical confirmations for the asymptotic profile described in Theorem 4. For this purpose, we propose a new mesh-refinement method inspired by the rescaling algorithm of Berger and Kohn [5]. Note that, their method was successful to solve blowing-up problems which are invariant under the following transformation,

∀γ>0,γ↦uγ​(ξ,τ)=γ2p−1​u​(γ​ξ,γ2​τ).\forall\gamma>0,\quad\gamma\mapsto u_{\gamma}(\xi,\tau)=\gamma^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u(\gamma\xi,\gamma^{2}\tau). (26)

However, there are a lot of equations whose solutions blow up in finite time but the equation does not satisfy the property (26), one of them is the equation (1) because of the presence of the perturbation term hh. Although our method is very similar to Berger and Kohn’s algorithm in spirit, it is better in the sense that it can be applied to a larger class of blowing-up problems which do not satisfy the rescaling property (26). Up to our knowledge, there are not many papers on the numerical blow-up profile, apart from the paper of Berger and Kohn [5] (see also [31]), who already obtained numerical results for equation (1) without the perturbation term. For other numerical aspects, there are several studies for (1) in the unperturbed case, see for example, Abia, López-Marcos and Martínez in [2], [1], Groisman and Rossi [17],[18], [16], N’gohisse and Boni [30], Kyza and Makridakis [26], Cangiani et al. [7] and the references therein. There is also the work of Baruch et al. [4] studying standing-ring solutions.

This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1. Theorem 2 follows from Theorem 1. Since all the arguments presented [32] remain valid for the case (7), except the existence of the Lyapunov functional for equation (9) (Theorem 1), we kindly refer the reader to Section 2.3 and 2.4 in [32] for details of the proof. Section 3 deals with results on asymptotic behaviors (Theorem 3 and Theorem 4). In Section 4, we describe the new mesh-refinement method and give some numerical justifications for the theoretical results.

Acknowledgement: The authors are grateful to M. A. Hamza for several helpful conversations pertaining to this work, and especially for giving the idea for the proof of Theorem 1 in this paper.

3 Blow-up behavior

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 3 and Theorem 4. Consider bb a blow-up point and write ww instead of wb,Tw_{b,T} for simplicity. From (i​i)(ii) of Theorem 2 and up to changing the signs of ww and hh, we may assume that ‖w⁡(y,s)−κ‖Lρ2→0\|w(y,s)-\kappa\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}\to 0 as s→+∞s\to+\infty, uniformly on compact subsets of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. As mentioned in the introduction, by setting v⁡(y,s)=w⁡(y,s)−ϕ⁡(s)v(y,s)=w(y,s)-\phi(s) (ϕ\phi is the positive solution of (18) such that ϕ⁡(s)→κ\phi(s)\to\kappa as s→+∞s\to+\infty), we see that ‖v⁡(y,s)‖Lρ2→0\|v(y,s)\|_{L^{2}_{\rho}}\to 0 as s→+∞s\to+\infty and vv solves the following equation:

∂sv=(ℒ+ω(s))v+F(v)+G(v,s),∀y∈ℝn,∀s∈[−logT,+∞),\partial_{s}v=(\mathcal{L}+\omega(s))v+F(v)+G(v,s),\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\;\forall s\in[-\log T,+\infty), (33)

where ℒ=Δ−y2⋅∇+1\mathcal{L}=\Delta-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla+1 and ω\omega, FF, GG are given by

We now give the proof of Theorem 4 from Theorem 3. Note that the derivation of Theorem 4 from Theorem 3 in the unperturbed case (h≡0h\equiv 0) was done by Velázquez in [34]. The idea to extend the convergence up to sets of the type {|y|≤K0s}\{|y|\leq K_{0}\sqrt{s}\} or {|y|≤K0e(12−1m)​s}\{|y|\leq K_{0}e^{\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{m}\right)s}\} is to estimate the effect of the convective term −y2⋅∇w-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla w in the equation (9) in LρqL^{q}_{\rho} spaces with q>1q>1. Since the proof of Theorem 4 is actually in spirit by the method given in [34], all that we need to do is to control the strong perturbation term in equation (9). We therefore give the main steps of the proof and focus only on the new arguments. Note also that we only give the proof of OPENi​i)ii) of Theorem 3 because the proof of OPENi​i​i)iii) is exactly the same as written in Proposition 34 in [32].

4 Numerical method

We give in this section a numerical study of the blow-up profile of equation (1) in one dimension. Though our method is very similar to Berger and Kohn’s algorithm [5] in spirit, it is better in the sense that is can be applied to equations which are not invariant under the transformation (26). Our method differs from Berger and Kohn’s in the following way: we step the solution forward until its maximum value multiplied by a power of its mesh size reaches a preset threshold, where the mesh size and the preset threshold are linked; for the rescaling algorithm, the solution is stepped forward until its maximum value reaches a preset threshold, and the mesh size and the preset threshold do not need to be linked. For more clarity, we present in the next subsection the mesh-refinement technique applied to equation (1), then give various numerical experiments to illustrate the effectiveness of our method for the problem of the numerical blow-up profile. Note that our method is more general than Berger and Kohn’s [5], in the sense that it applies to non scale invariant equations. However, when applied to the unperturbed case F⁡(u)=|u|p−1​uF(u)=|u|^{p-1}u, our method gives exactly the same approximation as that of [5].

4.1 Mesh-refinement algorithm

In this section, we describe our refinement algorithm to solve numerically the problem (1) with initial data φ⁡(x)>0\varphi(x)>0, φ⁡(x)=φ⁡(−x)\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x), x​d​φ​(x)d​x<0x\frac{d\varphi(x)}{dx}<0 for x≠0x\neq 0, which gives a positive symmetric and radially decreasing solution. Let us rewrite the problem (1) (with μ=1\mu=1) in the following:

{ut=ux​x+F⁡(u),(x,t)∈(−1,1)×(0,T),u⁡(1,t)=u(−1,t)=0,t∈(0,T),u⁡(x,0)=φ⁡(x),x∈(−1,1),\left\{\begin{array}[]{lrl}u_{t}&=&u_{xx}+F(u),\quad(x,t)\in(-1,1)\times(0,T),\\ u(1,t)&=&u(-1,t)=0,\quad t\in(0,T),\\ u(x,0)&=&\varphi(x),\quad x\in(-1,1),\end{array}\right. (43)

where p>1p>1 and

F⁡(u)=up+uploga⁡(2+u2)with​a>0.F(u)=u^{p}+\frac{u^{p}}{\log^{a}(2+u^{2})}\quad\text{with}\;\;a>0. (44)

Let ℏ\hbar and τ\tau be the initial space and time steps, we define CΔ=τℏ2C_{\Delta}=\frac{\tau}{\hbar^{2}}, xi=i​ℏx^{i}=i\hbar, tn=n​τt^{n}=n\tau, I=1ℏI=\frac{1}{\hbar} and ui,nu^{i,n} as the approximation of u⁡(xi,tn)u(x^{i},t^{n}), where ui,nu^{i,n} is defined for all n≥0n\geq 0, for all i∈{−I,…,I}i\in\{-I,\dots,I\} by

ui,n+1=ui,n+CΔ​[ui−1,n−2​ui,n+ui+1,n]+τ​F​(ui,n),\displaystyle u^{i,n+1}=u^{i,n}+C_{\Delta}\left[u^{i-1,n}-2u^{i,n}+u^{i+1,n}\right]+\tau F\left(u^{i,n}\right), (45)
uI,n=u−I,n=0,ui,0=φi.\displaystyle u^{I,n}=u^{-I,n}=0,\quad u^{i,0}=\varphi_{i}.

Note that this scheme is first order accurate in time and second order in space, and it requests the stability condition CΔ=τℏ2≤12C_{\Delta}=\frac{\tau}{\hbar^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{2}.
Our algorithm needs to fix the following parameters:

  • 1.

    λ<1\lambda<1: the refining factor with λ−1\lambda^{-1} being a small integer.

  • 2.

    MM: the threshold to control the amplitude of the solution,

  • 3.

    α\alpha: the parameter controlling the width of interval to be refined.

The parameters λ\lambda and MM must satisfy the following relation:

M=λ−2p−1​M0,whereM0=ℏ2p−1​‖φ‖∞.M=\lambda^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}M_{0},\quad\text{where}\quad M_{0}=\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|\varphi\|_{\infty}. (46)

Note that the relation (46) is important to make our method works. In [5], the typical choice is M0=‖φ‖∞M_{0}=\|\varphi\|_{\infty}, hence M=λ−2p−1​‖φ‖∞M=\lambda^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}\|\varphi\|_{\infty}.

In the initial step of the algorithm, we simply apply the scheme (45) until ℏ2p−1​‖u⁡(∙,tn)‖∞\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u(\centerdot,t^{n})\|_{\infty} reaches MM (note that in [5] the solution is stepped forward until ‖u⁡(∙,tn)‖∞\|u(\centerdot,t^{n})\|_{\infty} reaches MM; in this first step, the thresholds of the two methods are the same, however, they will split after the second step; roughly speaking, for the threshold we shall use the quantity ℏ2p−1​‖u⁡(∙,tn)‖∞\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u(\centerdot,t^{n})\|_{\infty} in our method instead of ‖u⁡(∙,tn)‖∞\|u(\centerdot,t^{n})\|_{\infty} in [5]). Then, we use a linear interpolation in time to find τ0∗\tau_{0}^{*} such that

tn−τ≤τ0∗≤tnandℏ2p−1​‖u⁡(∙,τ0∗)‖=M.t^{n}-\tau\leq\tau_{0}^{*}\leq t^{n}\quad\text{and}\quad\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u(\centerdot,\tau_{0}^{*})\|=M.

Afterward, we determine two grid points y0−y_{0}^{-} and y0+y_{0}^{+} such that

{ℏ2p−1​u​(y0−−ℏ,τ0∗)<α​M≤ℏ2p−1​u​(y0−,τ0∗)ℏ2p−1​u​(y0++ℏ,τ0∗)<α​M≤ℏ2p−1​u​(y0+,τ0∗).\left\{\begin{aligned} &\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u(y_{0}^{-}-\hbar,\tau_{0}^{*})<\alpha M\leq\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u(y_{0}^{-},\tau_{0}^{*})\\ &\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u(y_{0}^{+}+\hbar,\tau_{0}^{*})<\alpha M\leq\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u(y_{0}^{+},\tau_{0}^{*}).\end{aligned}\right. (47)

Note that y0−=−y0+y_{0}^{-}=-y_{0}^{+} because of the symmetry of the solution. This closes the initial step.

Let us begin the first refining step. Define

u1​(y1,t1)=u⁡(y1,τ0∗+t1),y1∈(y0−,y0+),t1≥0,u_{1}(y_{1},t_{1})=u(y_{1},\tau_{0}^{*}+t_{1}),\quad y_{1}\in(y_{0}^{-},y_{0}^{+}),\;t_{1}\geq 0, (48)

and setting h1=λ​ℏh_{1}=\lambda\hbar, τ1=λ2​τ\tau_{1}=\lambda^{2}\tau as the space and time step for the approximation of u1u_{1} (note that τ1h12=τℏ2=CΔ\frac{\tau_{1}}{h_{1}^{2}}=\frac{\tau}{\hbar^{2}}=C_{\Delta} which is a constant), y1i=i​h1y_{1}^{i}=ih_{1}, t1n=n​τ1t_{1}^{n}=n\tau_{1}, I1=y0+h1I_{1}=\frac{y_{0}^{+}}{h_{1}} and u1i,nu_{1}^{i,n} as the approximation of u1​(y1i,t1n)u_{1}(y_{1}^{i},t_{1}^{n}) (note that in the unperturbed case, Berger and Kohn used the transformation (26) to define u1​(y1,t1)=λ2p−1​u​(λ​y1,τ0∗+λ2​t1)u_{1}(y_{1},t_{1})=\lambda^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u(\lambda y_{1},\tau_{0}^{*}+\lambda^{2}t_{1}), and then applied the same scheme for uu to u1u_{1}. However, we can not do the same because the equation (43) is not in fact invariant under the transformation (26)). Then applying the scheme (45) to u1u_{1} which reads

u1i,n+1=u1i,n+CΔ​[u1i−1,n−2​u1i,n+u1i+1,n]+τ1​F​(u1i,n),\displaystyle u_{1}^{i,n+1}=u_{1}^{i,n}+C_{\Delta}\left[u_{1}^{i-1,n}-2u_{1}^{i,n}+u_{1}^{i+1,n}\right]+\tau_{1}F\left(u_{1}^{i,n}\right), (49)

for all n≥0n\geq 0 and for all i∈{−I1+1,…,I1−1}i\in\{-I_{1}+1,\dots,I_{1}-1\}.
Note that the computation of u1u_{1} requires the initial data u1​(y1,0)u_{1}(y_{1},0) and the boundary condition u1​(y0±,t1)u_{1}(y_{0}^{\pm},t_{1}). For the initial condition, it is determined from u⁡(x,τ0∗)u(x,\tau_{0}^{*}) by using interpolation in space to get values at the new grid points. For the boundary condition, since τ1=λ2​τ\tau_{1}=\lambda^{2}\tau, we then have from (48),

u1​(y0±,n​τ1)=u⁡(y0±,τ0∗+n​λ2​τ).u_{1}(y_{0}^{\pm},n\tau_{1})=u(y_{0}^{\pm},\tau_{0}^{*}+n\lambda^{2}\tau). (50)

Since uu and u1u_{1} will be stepped forward, each on its own grid (u1u_{1} on (y0​⁻,y0+)(y_{0}⁻,y_{0}^{+}) with the space and time step h1h_{1} and τ1\tau_{1}, and uu on (−1,1)(-1,1) with the space and time step ℏ\hbar and τ\tau), the relation (50) will provide us with the boundary values for u1u_{1}. In order to better understand how it works, let us consider an example with λ=12\lambda=\frac{1}{2}. After closing the initial phase, the two solutions u1u_{1} and uu are stepped forward independently, each on its own grid, in other words, u1u_{1} on (y0​⁻,y0+)(y_{0}⁻,y_{0}^{+}) with the space and time step h1h_{1} and τ1\tau_{1}, and uu on (−1,1)(-1,1) with the space and time step ℏ\hbar and τ\tau. Then using the linear interpolation in time for uu, we get the boundary values for u1u_{1} by (50). Since τ1=λ2​τ=14​τ\tau_{1}=\lambda^{2}\tau=\frac{1}{4}\tau. This means that uu is stepped forward once every 4 time steps of u1u_{1}. After 4 steps forward of u1u_{1}, the values of uu on the interval (y0−,y0+)(y_{0}^{-},y_{0}^{+}) must be updated to agree with the calculations of u1u_{1}. In other words, the approximation of uu is used to assist in computing the boundary values for u1u_{1}. At each successive time step for uu, the values of uu on the interval (y0−,y0+)(y_{0}^{-},y_{0}^{+}) must be updated to make them agree with the more accurate fine grid solution u1u_{1}. When h12p−1​‖u1​(∙,n​τ1)‖∞h_{1}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u_{1}(\centerdot,n\tau_{1})\|_{\infty} first exceeds MM, we use a linear interpolation in time to find τ1∗∈[τ1n−1,τ1n]\tau_{1}^{*}\in[\tau_{1}^{n-1},\tau_{1}^{n}] such that h12p−1​‖u1​(∙,τ1∗)‖∞=Mh_{1}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u_{1}(\centerdot,\tau_{1}^{*})\|_{\infty}=M. On the interval where h12p−1​‖u1​(∙,τ1∗)‖∞>α​Mh_{1}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u_{1}(\centerdot,\tau_{1}^{*})\|_{\infty}>\alpha M, the grid is refined further and the entire procedure as for u1u_{1} is repeated to yield u2u_{2} and so forth.

Before going to a general step, we would like to comment on the relation (46). Indeed, when ℏ2p−1​‖u⁡(∙,t)‖∞\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u(\centerdot,t)\|_{\infty} reaches the given threshold MM in the initial phase, namely when ℏ2p−1​‖u⁡(∙,τ0∗)‖∞=M\hbar^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u(\centerdot,\tau_{0}^{*})\|_{\infty}=M, we want to refine the grid such that the maximum values of h12p−1​u1​(y1,0)h_{1}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u_{1}(y_{1},0) equals to M0M_{0}. By (48), this request turns into h12p−1​‖u⁡(∙,τ0∗)‖∞=M0h_{1}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u(\centerdot,\tau_{0}^{*})\|_{\infty}=M_{0}. Since h1=λ​ℏh_{1}=\lambda\hbar, it follows that M=λ−2p−1​M0M=\lambda^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}M_{0}, which yields (46).

Let k≥0k\geq 0, we set hk+1=λ−1​hkh_{k+1}=\lambda^{-1}h_{k} and τk+1=λ2​τk\tau_{k+1}=\lambda^{2}\tau_{k} (note that τk+1hk+12=τkhk2=CΔ\frac{\tau_{k+1}}{h_{k+1}^{2}}=\frac{\tau_{k}}{h_{k}^{2}}=C_{\Delta} which is a constant), yk+1y_{k+1} and tk+1t_{k+1} as the variables of uk+1u_{k+1}, yki=i​hky_{k}^{i}=ih_{k}, tkn=n​τkt_{k}^{n}=n\tau_{k}. The index k=0k=0 means that u0​(y0,t0)≡u⁡(x,t)u_{0}(y_{0},t_{0})\equiv u(x,t), h0≡ℏh_{0}\equiv\hbar and τ0≡τ\tau_{0}\equiv\tau. The solution uk+1u_{k+1} is related to uku_{k} by

uk+1​(yk+1,tk+1)=uk​(yk+1,τk∗+tk+1),yk+1∈(yk−,yk+),tk+1≥0.u_{k+1}(y_{k+1},t_{k+1})=u_{k}(y_{k+1},\tau_{k}^{*}+t_{k+1}),\quad y_{k+1}\in(y_{k}^{-},y_{k}^{+}),\;t_{k+1}\geq 0. (51)

Here, the time τk∗∈[tkn−1,tkn]\tau_{k}^{*}\in[t_{k}^{n-1},t_{k}^{n}] satisfies hk2p−1​‖uk​(⋅,τk∗)‖∞=Mh_{k}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u_{k}(\cdot,\tau_{k}^{*})\|_{\infty}=M, and yk−,yk+y_{k}^{-},y_{k}^{+} are two grid points determined by

{hk2p−1​uk​(yk−−hk,τk∗)<α​M≤hk2p−1​uk​(yk−,τk∗),hk2p−1​uk​(yk++hk,τk∗)<α​M≤hk2p−1​uk​(yk+,τk∗).\left\{\begin{aligned} &h_{k}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u_{k}(y_{k}^{-}-h_{k},\tau_{k}^{*})<\alpha M\leq h_{k}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u_{k}(y_{k}^{-},\tau_{k}^{*}),\\ &h_{k}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u_{k}(y_{k}^{+}+h_{k},\tau_{k}^{*})<\alpha M\leq h_{k}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u_{k}(y_{k}^{+},\tau_{k}^{*}).\end{aligned}\right. (52)

The approximation of uk+1​(yk+1i,tk+1n)u_{k+1}(y_{k+1}^{i},t_{k+1}^{n}) (denoted by uk+1i,nu_{k+1}^{i,n}) uses the scheme (45) with the space step hk+1h_{k+1} and the time step τk+1\tau_{k+1}, which reads

uk+1i,n+1\displaystyle u_{k+1}^{i,n+1} =uk+1i,n+CΔ​[uk+1i−1,n−2​uk+1i,n+uk+1i+1,n]+τk+1​F​(uk+1i,n),\displaystyle=u_{k+1}^{i,n}+C_{\Delta}\left[u_{k+1}^{i-1,n}-2u_{k+1}^{i,n}+u_{k+1}^{i+1,n}\right]+\tau_{k+1}F\left(u_{k+1}^{i,n}\right), (53)

for all n≥1n\geq 1 and i∈{−Ik+1,⋯,Ik−1}i\in\{-I_{k}+1,\cdots,I_{k}-1\} with Ik=yk+hk+1I_{k}=\frac{y_{k}^{+}}{h_{k+1}} (note from introduction that IkI_{k} is an integer since λ−1∈ℕ\lambda^{-1}\in\mathbb{N}).
As for the approximation of uku_{k}, the computation of uk+1i,nu_{k+1}^{i,n} needs the initial data and the boundary condition. From (51) and the fact that τk+1=λ2​τk\tau_{k+1}=\lambda^{2}\tau_{k}, we see that

uk+1​(yk+1,0)=uk​(yk+1,τk∗)anduk+1​(yk±,n​τk+1)=uk​(yk±,τk∗+n​λ2​τk).u_{k+1}(y_{k+1},0)=u_{k}(y_{k+1},\tau_{k}^{*})\quad\text{and}\quad u_{k+1}(y_{k}^{\pm},n\tau_{k+1})=u_{k}(y_{k}^{\pm},\tau_{k}^{*}+n\lambda^{2}\tau_{k}). (54)

Hence, from the first identity in (54), the initial data is simply calculated from uk​(⋅,τk∗)u_{k}(\cdot,\tau_{k}^{*}) by using a linear interpolation in space in order to assign values at new grid points. The essential step in this new mesh-refinement method is to determine the boundary condition through the second identity in (54). This means by a linear interpolation in time of uku_{k}. Therefore, the previous solutions uku_{k}, uk−1u_{k-1}, ⋯\cdots are stepped forward independently, each on its own grid. More precisely, since τk+1=λ2​τk=λ4​τk−1=⋯\tau_{k+1}=\lambda^{2}\tau_{k}=\lambda^{4}\tau_{k-1}=\cdots, then uku_{k} is stepped forward once every λ−2\lambda^{-2} time steps of uk+1u_{k+1}; uk−1u_{k-1} once every λ−4\lambda^{-4} time steps of uk+1u_{k+1}, … On the other hand, the values of uku_{k}, uk−1u_{k-1}, … must be updated to agree with the calculation of uk+1u_{k+1}. When hk+12p−1​‖uk+1​(∙,τk+1)‖∞>Mh_{k+1}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u_{k+1}(\centerdot,\tau_{k+1})\|_{\infty}>M, then it is time for the next refining phase.

We would like to comment on the output of the refinement algorithm:

  • i)

    Let τk∗\tau_{k}^{*} be the time at which the refining takes place, then the ratio τk∗τk\frac{\tau_{k}^{*}}{\tau_{k}}, which indicates the number of time steps until hk2p−1​‖uk‖∞h_{k}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u_{k}\|_{\infty}, reaches the given threshold MM, is independent of kk and tends to a constant as k→∞k\to\infty.

  • ii)

    Let uk​(⋅,τk∗)u_{k}(\cdot,\tau_{k}^{*}) be the refining solution. If we plot hk2p−1​uk​(∙,τk∗)h_{k}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}u_{k}(\centerdot,\tau_{k}^{*}) on (−1,1)(-1,1), then their graphs are eventually independent of kk and converge as k→∞k\to\infty.

  • iii)

    Let (yk−,yk+)(y_{k}^{-},y_{k}^{+}) be the interval to be refined, then the quality (hk−1​yk+)2(h_{k}^{-1}y_{k}^{+})^{2} behaves as a linear function of kk.

These assertions can be well understood by the following theorem:

Theorem 11 (Formal analysis).

Let uu be a blowing-up solution to equation (43), then the output of the refinement algorithm satisfies:

where γ=2​M1−p​(α1−p−1)​|log⁡λ|cp​(p−1)​λ2\gamma=\frac{2M^{1-p}(\alpha^{1-p}-1)|\log\lambda|}{c_{p}(p-1)\lambda^{2}}, B=−M1−p​(α1−p−1)cp​(p−1)​λ2​log⁡(M1−p​ℏ2p−1)B=-\frac{M^{1-p}(\alpha^{1-p}-1)}{c_{p}(p-1)\lambda^{2}}\log\left(\frac{M^{1-p}\hbar^{2}}{p-1}\right) and cp=p−14​pc_{p}=\frac{p-1}{4p} .

4.2 The numerical results

This subsection gives various numerical confirmation for the assertions stated in the previous subsection (Theorem 11). All the experiments reported here used φ⁡(x)=2​(1+c​o​s​(π​x))\varphi(x)=2(1+cos(\pi x)) as the initial data, α=0.6\alpha=0.6 as the parameter for controlling the interval to be refined, λ=12\lambda=\frac{1}{2} as the refining factor, CΔ=14C_{\Delta}=\frac{1}{4} as the stability condition for the scheme (45), p=3p=3 and a=0.1,1,10a=0.1,1,10 in the nonlinearity FF given in (44). The threshold MM is chosen to be satisfied the condition (46). In Table 4.1, we give some values of MM corresponding the initial data and the initial space step ℏ\hbar.

We generally stop the computation after 4040 refining phases. Indeed, since hk2p−1​‖uk​(∙,τk∗)‖∞=Mh_{k}^{\frac{2}{p-1}}\|u_{k}(\centerdot,\tau_{k}^{*})\|_{\infty}=M and the fact that hk=λ​hk−1h_{k}=\lambda h_{k-1}, we have by induction,

‖uk​(∙,τk∗)‖∞=hk−2p−1​M=(λ​hk−1)−2p−1​M=⋯=(λk​ℏ)−2p−1​M.\|u_{k}(\centerdot,\tau_{k}^{*})\|_{\infty}=h_{k}^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}M=(\lambda h_{k-1})^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}M=\dots=(\lambda^{k}\hbar)^{-\frac{2}{p-1}}M.

With these parameters, we see that the corresponding amplitude of uu approaches 101210^{12} after 4040 iterations.

OPENi)i) The value τk∗τk\frac{\tau^{*}_{k}}{\tau_{k}} is independent of kk and tends to the constant as k→+∞k\to+\infty.
It is convenient to denote the computed value of τk∗τk\frac{\tau_{k}^{*}}{\tau_{k}} by NkN_{k} and the predicted value given in the statement OPENi)i) of Theorem 11 by Np​r​eN_{pre}. Note that the values of Np​r​eN_{pre} does not depend on aa but depend on ℏ\hbar because of the relation (46). More precisely,

Np​r​e​(ℏ)=(1−λ2)​‖φ‖∞1−pCΔ​(p−1)​ℏ2.N_{pre}(\hbar)=\frac{(1-\lambda^{2})\|\varphi\|_{\infty}^{1-p}}{C_{\Delta}(p-1)\hbar^{2}}.

Then considering the quality NkNp​r​e\frac{N_{k}}{N_{pre}}, theoretically, it is expected to converge to 11 as kk tends to infinity. Table 4.2 provides computed values of NkNp​r​e\frac{N_{k}}{N_{pre}} at some selected indexes of kk, for computing with ℏ=0.005\hbar=0.005 and three different values of aa. According to the numerical results given in Table 4.2, the computed values in the case a=10a=10 and a=1.0a=1.0 approach to 11 as expected which gives us a numerical answer for the statement (59). However the numerical results in the case a=0.1a=0.1 is not good due to the fact that the speech of convergence to the blow-up limit (59) is 1|log⁡(T−t)|a′\frac{1}{|\log(T-t)|^{a^{\prime}}} with a′=min⁡{a,1}a^{\prime}=\min\{a,1\} (see Theorem 3).

OPENi​i)ii) The function vk​(z)v_{k}(z) introduced in part 𝐎𝐏𝐄𝐍i​i)ii) of Theorem 11 converges to a predicted profile as k→+∞k\to+\infty.
As stated in part OPENi​i)ii) of Theorem 11, if we plot vk​(z)v_{k}(z) over the fixed interval (−1,1)(-1,1), then the graph of vkv_{k} would converge to the predicted one. Figure 1 gives us a numerical confirmation for this fact, for computing with ℏ=0.005\hbar=0.005 and a=10a=10. Looking at Figure 1, we see that the graph of vkv_{k} evidently converges to the predicted one given in the right-hand side of (56) as kk increases. The last curve v40v_{40} seemly coincides to the prediction. Figure 2 shows the graph of v40v_{40} and the predicted profile for an other experiment with ℏ=0.005\hbar=0.005 and a=0.1a=0.1. They coincide to within plotting resolution.

In Table 4.3, we give the error in L∞L^{\infty} between vk​(z)v_{k}(z) at index k=40k=40 and the predicted profile given in the right hand-side of (56), namely

eℏ,a=supz∈(−1,1)|v40​(z)−M​(1+(α1−p−1)​λ−2​z2)−1p−1|.e_{\hbar,a}=\sup_{z\in(-1,1)}\left|v_{40}(z)-M\left(1+(\alpha^{1-p}-1)\lambda^{-2}z^{2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\right|. (67)

These numerical computations give us a confirmation that the computed profiles vkv_{k} converges to the predicted one. Since the error eℏ,ae_{\hbar,a} tends to 00 as ℏ\hbar goes to zero, the numerical computations also answer to the stability of the blow-up profile stated in OPENi)i) of Theorem 4. In fact, the stability makes the solution visible in numerical simulations.

OPENi​i​i)iii) The quality (hk−1​yk+)2(h_{k}^{-1}y_{k}^{+})^{2} behaves like a linear function.
For making a quantitative comparison between our numerical results and the predicted behavior as stated in OPENi​i​i)iii) of Theorem 11, we plot the graph of (hk−1​yk+)2(h_{k}^{-1}y_{k}^{+})^{2} against kk and denote by γℏ,a\gamma_{\hbar,a} the slope of this curve. Then considering the ratio γℏ,aγ\frac{\gamma_{\hbar,a}}{\gamma}, where γ\gamma is given in part OPENi​i​i)iii) of Theorem 11. As expected, this ratio γℏ,aγ\frac{\gamma_{\hbar,a}}{\gamma} would approach one. Figure 3 shows (hk−1​yk+)2(h_{k}^{-1}y_{k}^{+})^{2} as a function of kk for computing with the initial space step ℏ=0.005\hbar=0.005 for different values of aa. Looking at Figure 3, we see that the two middle curves corresponding the case a=10a=10 and a=1a=1 behave like the predicted linear function (the top line), while this is not true in the case a=0.1a=0.1 (the bottom curve). In order to make this clearer, let us see Table 4.4 which lists the values of γℏ,aγ\frac{\gamma_{\hbar,a}}{\gamma} for computing with various values of the initial space step ℏ\hbar for three different values of aa. Here, the value of γℏ,a\gamma_{\hbar,a} is calculated for 20≤k≤4020\leq k\leq 40. As Table 4.4 shows that the numerical values in the case a=10a=10 and a=1a=1 agree with the prediction stated in OPENi​i)ii) of Theorem 11, while the numerical values in the case a=0.1a=0.1 is far from the predicted one.

Appendix A Appendix A

The following lemma from [32] gives the expansion of ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s), the unique solution of equation (18) satisfying (19):

Lemma A.1.

Let ϕ\phi be a positive solution of the following ordinary differential equation:

ϕs=−ϕp−1+ϕp+μ​ϕploga⁡(2+e2​sp−1​ϕ2).\phi_{s}=-\frac{\phi}{p-1}+\phi^{p}+\frac{\mu\phi^{p}}{\log^{a}(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2})}.

Assuming in addition ϕ⁡(s)→κ\phi(s)\to\kappa as s→+∞s\to+\infty, then ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s) takes the following form:

ϕ⁡(s)=κ​(1+ηa​(s))−1p−1ass→+∞,\phi(s)=\kappa(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}\quad\text{as}\quad s\to+\infty,

where

ηa​(s)∼C∗​∫s+∞es−ττa​𝑑τ=C∗sa​(1+∑j≥1bjsj),\eta_{a}(s)\sim C_{*}\int_{s}^{+\infty}\frac{e^{s-\tau}}{\tau^{a}}d\tau=\frac{C_{*}}{s^{a}}\left(1+\sum_{j\geq 1}\frac{b_{j}}{s^{j}}\right),

with C∗=μ​(p−12)aC_{*}=\mu\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)^{a} and bj=(−1)j​∏i=0j−1(a+i)b_{j}=(-1)^{j}\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}(a+i).

Proof.

See Lemma A.3 in [32]. ∎

Appendix B Appendix B

We aim at proving the following:

Lemma B.1 (Estimate of ω⁡(s)\omega(s)).

We have

|ω⁡(s)|=𝒪⁡(1sa+1),ass→+∞.|\omega(s)|=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}\right),\quad\text{as}\quad s\to+\infty.
Proof.

From Lemma A.1, we write

p⁡(ϕ​(s)p−1−κp−1)=−p​ηa​(s)p−1​(1+ηa​(s))−1=−p​C∗(p−1)​sa​(1+ηa​(s))−1+𝒪⁡(1sa+1).p(\phi(s)^{p-1}-\kappa^{p-1})=-\frac{p\eta_{a}(s)}{p-1}(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-1}=-\frac{pC_{*}}{(p-1)s^{a}}(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-1}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}\right).

A direct calculation yields,

e−s​h′​(epp−1​ϕ​(s))\displaystyle e^{-s}h^{\prime}\left(e^{\frac{p}{p-1}}\phi(s)\right) =μ​p​ϕp−1​(s)loga⁡(2+e2​sp−1​ϕ2​(s))−2​a​μ​e2​sp−1​ϕp+1​(s)(2+e2​sp−1​ϕ2​(s))​loga+1⁡(2+e2​sp−1​ϕ2​(s))\displaystyle=\frac{\mu p\phi^{p-1}(s)}{\log^{a}(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2}(s))}-\frac{2a\mu e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{p+1}(s)}{(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2}(s))\log^{a+1}(2+e^{\frac{2s}{p-1}}\phi^{2}(s))}
=p​C∗(p−1)​sa​(1+ηa​(s))−1+𝒪⁡(1sa+1).\displaystyle=\frac{pC_{*}}{(p-1)s^{a}}(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-1}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{s^{a+1}}\right).

Adding the two above estimates, we obtain the desired result. This ends the proof of Lemma B.1. ∎

Lemma B.2 (Estimate of R⁡(y,s)R(y,s)).

We have

|R⁡(y,s)|=𝒪⁡(|y|2+1sa′+1),ass→+∞,|R(y,s)|=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{|y|^{2}+1}{s^{a^{\prime}+1}}\right),\quad\text{as}\quad s\to+\infty,

with a′=min⁡{1,a}a^{\prime}=\min\{1,a\}.

Proof.

Let us write φ⁡(y,s)=ϕ⁡(s)κ​ν​(y,s)\varphi(y,s)=\frac{\phi(s)}{\kappa}\nu(y,s) where

ν⁡(y,s)=κ​(1+p−14​p​s​∑j=1lyj2)−1p−1+κ​l2​p​s.\nu(y,s)=\kappa\left(1+\frac{p-1}{4ps}\sum_{j=1}^{l}y_{j}^{2}\right)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}+\frac{\kappa l}{2ps}.

Then, we write R⁡(y,s)=ϕ⁡(s)κ​R1​(y,s)+R2​(y,s)R(y,s)=\frac{\phi(s)}{\kappa}R_{1}(y,s)+R_{2}(y,s) where

R1​(y,s)\displaystyle R_{1}(y,s) =νs−Δ​ν−y2⋅∇ν−νp−1+νp,\displaystyle=\nu_{s}-\Delta\nu-\frac{y}{2}\cdot\nabla\nu-\frac{\nu}{p-1}+\nu^{p},
R2​(y,s)\displaystyle R_{2}(y,s) =−ϕ′κ​ν−ϕκ​νp+ϕp​(νκ)p+e−p​sp−1​h′​(esp−1​ϕ​νκ).\displaystyle=-\frac{\phi^{\prime}}{\kappa}\nu-\frac{\phi}{\kappa}\nu^{p}+\phi^{p}\left(\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)^{p}+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h^{\prime}\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\frac{\phi\nu}{\kappa}\right).

The term R1​(y,s)R_{1}(y,s) is already treated in [34], and it is bounded by

|R1(y,s)|≤C⁡(|y|2+1)s2+C𝟏{|y|≥2K0s}.|R_{1}(y,s)|\leq\frac{C(|y|^{2}+1)}{s^{2}}+C\mathbf{1}_{\{|y|\geq 2K_{0}\sqrt{s}\}}.

To bound R2R_{2}, we use the fact that ϕ\phi satisfies (19) to write

R2​(y,s)\displaystyle R_{2}(y,s) =ν​ϕκp​(κp−1−ϕp−1)​(κp−1−νp−1)\displaystyle=\frac{\nu\phi}{\kappa^{p}}(\kappa^{p-1}-\phi^{p-1})(\kappa^{p-1}-\nu^{p-1})
+e−p​sp−1​[h⁡(esp−1​ϕ​νκ)−h⁡(esp−1​ϕ)]\displaystyle+e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}\left[h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\frac{\phi\nu}{\kappa}\right)-h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi\right)\right]
+(1−νκ)​e−p​sp−1​h​(esp−1​ϕ).\displaystyle+\left(1-\frac{\nu}{\kappa}\right)e^{-\frac{ps}{p-1}}h\left(e^{\frac{s}{p-1}}\phi\right).

Noting that ν⁡(y,s)=κ+ν¯​(y,s)\nu(y,s)=\kappa+\bar{\nu}(y,s) with |ν¯​(y,s)|≤Cs​(|y|2+1)|\bar{\nu}(y,s)|\leq\frac{C}{s}(|y|^{2}+1), uniformly for y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R} and s≥1s\geq 1, and recalling from Lemma A.1 that ϕ⁡(s)=κ​(1+ηa​(s))−1p−1\phi(s)=\kappa(1+\eta_{a}(s))^{-\frac{1}{p-1}} where ηa​(s)=𝒪⁡(s−a)\eta_{a}(s)=\mathcal{O}(s^{-a}), then using a Taylor expansion, we derive

|R2(y,s)|≤C(|y|2+1sa+1+𝟏{|y|≥2K0s}).|R_{2}(y,s)|\leq C\left(\frac{|y|^{2}+1}{s^{a+1}}+\mathbf{1}_{\{|y|\geq 2K_{0}\sqrt{s}\}}\right).

This concludes the proof of Lemma B.2. ∎
